units.passage: or any AI tools for content generation (spell-checkers are allowed)
units.why: "(spell-checkers are allowed)" exempts spell-checkers from the ban, P100.

units.passage: The use of AI systems for editing and grammar enhancement is common practice and, as such, is generally outside the intent of the above policy.
units.why: 'is common practice and, as such, is generally outside the intent of the above policy' exempts editing and grammar tools from the IEEE disclosure rule: P100.
units.fit_note: Also recommends disclosure.

units.passage: This includes AI features built into IDEs, operating systems, or browsers when they generate or substantially rewrite content, but excludes non-generative tools such as basic spell-check, grammar/syntax highlighting, and linters
units.why: It 'excludes non-generative tools such as basic spell-check, grammar/syntax highlighting, and linters', exempting routine features, P100.

units.passage: AI writing assistants that generate substantive content beyond basic grammar/spelling correction (e.g., NotebookLM)
units.why: The scope covers "AI writing assistants that generate substantive content beyond basic grammar/spelling correction", implicitly leaving basic grammar and spelling correction out. Nearest type is P100 (routine features exempt).
units.fit_note: Exemption is implied by the scope definition rather than stated as a rule.

units.passage: The instructor should consider whether grammar/style-checking software (e.g., Grammarly) is allowable.
units.why: Instructors "should consider whether grammar/style-checking software (e.g., Grammarly) is allowable", leaving routine tools to the instructor; closest is P100 (routine features) though it only asks them to decide.
units.fit_note: Does not exempt routine tools; it asks the instructor to decide on them. Leaves the exemption to the instructor rather than granting it.

units.passage: Faculty, employees, trainees, and academic visitors must fully disclose how and where they used GAI technology in their work. For example, in academic writing include a statement in the methods or acknowledgements section. For educational materials, note in slide footers or syllabi if AI assisted in generating content or images. c. Faculty, employees, trainees, and academic visitors do not have to disclose the use of GAI with UAMS AI Governance Committee-approved tools, dictation software, language translation, spelling/grammar/punctuation, formatting, alphabetizing items, and formatting of citations (e.g., converting an APA citation to an AMA citation).
units.why: Disclosure is not required for 'approved tools, dictation software, language translation, spelling/grammar/punctuation, formatting'. These routine features are exempt from the disclosure rule, so P100.
units.fit_note: Also exempts committee-approved tools from disclosure, beyond routine features.

units.passage: Not even one sentence, and not even to help you with English as a second language. Grammarly is fine.
units.policy: Grammarly is fine even though generative AI may not be used for any writing.
units.why: Extends the writing ban to ESL help yet says 'Grammarly is fine', i.e., routine grammar tools are exempt (P100).
units.fit_note: Names one specific tool as exempt.

units.passage: (Note: be sure to think through and address exceptions you’re willing to entertain; e.g., the Gemini summaries that pop up at the top of every Google search)
units.why: "be sure to think through and address exceptions you’re willing to entertain; e.g., the Gemini summaries" asks instructors to address routine embedded AI features such as search summaries, so P100 fits.
units.fit_note: A: Asks instructors to decide on such exceptions rather than exempting them. B: Instructs instructors to decide on exceptions for embedded AI search summaries.

units.passage: the AI search results that now pop up at the top of the screen in any Google search do not count as using AI for the purposes of this policy if you are searching something up for clarification/research purposes, but you should consult the original source to assess its validity.
units.why: "the AI search results that now pop up at the top of the screen in any Google search do not count as using AI" exempts routine search summaries, P100, with a caveat to check sources.
units.fit_note: Exemption is paired with a duty to check the original source.

units.passage: For spell-check and grammar-check functions, you are limited to the basic spell-check and grammar-check features that come pre-loaded with word processing software such as MS Word or Google Docs.
units.why: "you are limited to the basic spell-check and grammar-check features that come pre-loaded with word processing software" permits only built-in checkers; routine features exempt (P100).

units.passage: Use of AI that is embedded within larger software (e.g., predictive text sentence completions, auto-correct, spell check, etc.), does not need to be disclosed.
units.policy: Use of AI that is embedded within larger software (e.g., predictive text sentence completions, auto-correct, spell check, etc.), does not need to be disclosed.
units.why: "does not need to be disclosed" exempts AI embedded in software such as predictive text, auto-correct and spell check from the disclosure rule, which is P100.
units.fit_note: Exemption is from disclosure, not from a ban.

units.passage: You may also want to specify which tools don’t “count” as advanced automated tools like those mentioned in other pages e.g. spell-check, grammar check, slide design, autofill, etc.
units.why: "You may also want to specify which tools don't count as advanced automated tools ... e.g. spell-check, grammar check, slide design, autofill" exempts routine features from a ban, so P100; may.

units.passage: Users are generally not expected to acknowledge the use of GenAI tools for assistance with tasks such as grammatical editing, website copy, or generation of boilerplate language for letters, provided the content is reviewed before use, attribution is not otherwise required, and GenAI use is not prohibited
units.policy: Users are generally not expected to acknowledge GenAI use for grammatical editing, website copy, or boilerplate language for letters, provided the content is reviewed before use, attribution is not otherwise required, and GenAI use is not prohibited.
units.why: 'Users are generally not expected to acknowledge the use of GenAI tools for assistance with tasks such as grammatical editing' exempts routine uses from disclosure, P100 (with conditions: content reviewed, no other attribution requirement).
units.fit_note: Exemption holds only if content is reviewed, attribution is not otherwise required, and GenAI use is not prohibited.

units.passage: Exceptions include the grammar check and spellcheck options on your word-processing software or Grammarly grammar check (but not GrammarlyGO’s generative text option); these approved tools make suggestions for revising work that you have already generated and may be used with caution and with the understanding that you are, as always, ultimately responsible for the work you generate
units.why: English sample policy: 'Exceptions include the grammar check and spellcheck options on your word-processing software or Grammarly grammar check (but not GrammarlyGO's generative text option)' exempts routine tools, P100.

units.passage: With this in mind, for writing assignments for this course, you are allowed to use built-in spellcheck, grammar check, or Grammarly (without the generative AI feature) after you have already brainstormed and drafted your work
units.policy: With this in mind, for writing assignments for this course, you are allowed to use built-in spellcheck, grammar check, or Grammarly (without the generative AI feature) after you have already brainstormed and drafted your work.
units.why: English HNRS 190: 'you are allowed to use built-in spellcheck, grammar check, or Grammarly (without the generative AI feature)' exempts routine tools, P100.

units.passage: This excludes AI-supported tools providing spelling and grammar checks.
units.why: "This excludes AI-supported tools providing spelling and grammar checks" exempts routine features from the ban (P100).

units.passage: For routine communications such as ordinary emails or letters, formal disclosure of AI assistance is generally not required
units.why: Exempts routine communications from formal disclosure, close to P100 though it concerns routine uses and not embedded features.
units.fit_note: Exempts routine communications from disclosure unless authorship is significant. | Coder B: Exempts routine communications, not built-in features; stronger disclosure if authorship matters.

units.passage: You do not need to disclose minor uses such as spelling correction, sentence-level grammar correction, citation formatting
units.why: 'You do not need to disclose minor uses such as spelling correction, sentence-level grammar correction, citation formatting' unless required; exempts routine features, P100.
units.fit_note: Exempts routine uses from disclosure rather than from the rules as a whole.

units.passage: Grammar and spellchecking tools such as those integrated into MS Word may be used.
units.why: OSU example: 'Grammar and spellchecking tools such as those integrated into MS Word may be used.'; routine features exempt, P100.

units.passage: Acceptable “AI” programs include only the spelling and grammar checking features in the Microsoft Office products.
units.why: UT Tyler example allows 'only the spelling and grammar checking features in the Microsoft Office products' and bans Grammarly; P100.
units.fit_note: Narrow exemption; Grammarly is excluded.

units.passage: AI can be used to spellcheck and help with grammar. It should not be providing original thoughts.
units.why: "AI can be used to spellcheck and help with grammar. It should not be providing original thoughts." exempts routine editing help while barring original content, P100.
units.fit_note: Also states AI should not provide original thoughts.

units.passage: This may include when use of tools requires citation and when it merely is serving a formatting, editing function.
units.why: "when use of tools requires citation and when it merely is serving a formatting, editing function" tells instructors to discuss which uses need citation and which do not; P100 (routine editing exempt), with a discussion framing.
units.fit_note: A prompt to discuss where the line falls, not a stated exemption. Says the line between citation and editing varies by course; it does not exempt editing outright.

units.passage: Software excluded from the definition of Generative Artificial Intelligence would include legal research systems, word processing programs and their standard tools (e.g., spelling, grammar, and plagiarism checks) or automatic cite checkers— i.e., machine processes that do not create content but review human-created content for common errors or omissions —unless specifically identified as such by the instructor, supervisor, appropriate Vice Chancellor or the Chancellor
units.why: Software "excluded from the definition of Generative Artificial Intelligence" includes standard word-processor tools such as spelling, grammar and plagiarism checks, so routine features fall outside the rules: P100.
units.fit_note: Exemption can be overridden: "unless specifically identified as such by the instructor, supervisor, appropriate Vice Chancellor or the Chancellor". Exemption can be overridden if the instructor, supervisor, Vice Chancellor or Chancellor identifies the software otherwise.

units.passage: A complete ban disallows all of these uses, so it may be wise to carve out limited exceptions or limit a ban to AI-generated text or images
units.policy: It may be wise to carve out limited exceptions or limit a ban to AI-generated text or images.
units.why: "it may be wise to carve out limited exceptions or limit a ban to AI-generated text or images" advises that any ban keep exceptions for routine AI features, so P100.
units.fit_note: Advice to carve out limited exceptions to a ban, and (coder B, as separate UNCOVERED unit) to limit a ban to AI-generated text or images; the second scoping advice is not an exemption of routine features.

units.passage: Your instructor of this course should provide guidance regarding non-generative technologies, including translation and access software, spelling and grammar checkers,
units.why: Instructors 'should provide guidance regarding non-generative technologies, including translation and access software, spelling and grammar checkers'; routine features need separate guidance, so P100.
units.fit_note: Says instructors should give guidance on these tools, not that they are exempt. Instructors are told to give guidance on such tools rather than exempting them outright.

units.passage: Students should acknowledge the use of generative AI (other than incidental use) and default to disclosing such assistance when in doubt.
units.policy: Incidental use of generative AI does not need to be acknowledged.
units.why: "(other than incidental use)" exempts incidental use from acknowledgment, so minor AI use does not need disclosure. P100 (exempt routine features) is nearest; it does not name spell-check or similar features, hence the fit note.
units.fit_note: Exempts 'incidental use' generally rather than named routine features such as spell-check.

units.passage: However, disclosure is not necessary for minor tasks or when significant edits are made to the AI-generated output.
units.why: "disclosure is not necessary for minor tasks or when significant edits are made"; exempts minor use, nearest P100.
units.fit_note: Exempts minor tasks and heavily edited output, not named routine features.

units.passage: Students are free to use these apps to help with rephrasing sentences, rearranging paragraphs, grammar, etc., that are otherwise self-written.
units.why: The text says students 'are free to use these apps' such as Grammarly or Word spelling and grammar checkers 'to help with rephrasing sentences, rearranging paragraphs, grammar' for self-written text; routine writing-checker features are exempt, P100.

units.passage: core grammar and revision tools (spelling, clarity, fluency, tone) are reactive. They provide in-line suggestions based on what a student has already written, helping improve what’s there, but not writing it for them. These tools are typically viewed as learning aids
units.policy: Grammarly's core grammar and revision tools (spelling, clarity, fluency, tone) are reactive and typically viewed as learning aids, distinct from generative AI.
units.why: Grammarly's core grammar tools are "typically viewed as learning aids" and are reactive, unlike its generative tools. Routine embedded features are treated differently from generative AI, which P100 covers.
units.fit_note: Descriptive: it says the tools are viewed as learning aids and does not state an explicit exemption. Framed as how the tools are 'typically viewed', not as an explicit exemption.

units.passage: Basic grammar, spelling, and punctuation features are permitted unless they generate or substantially rewrite content
units.why: 'Basic grammar, spelling, and punctuation features are permitted unless they generate or substantially rewrite content' exempts routine features from the rules, P100.

units.passage: Basic grammar, spelling, and punctuation features, approved assistive technologies, and approved disability accommodations are permitted
units.why: Grammar, spelling and punctuation features, assistive tech 'are permitted unless they generate or substantially rewrite content': P100.
units.fit_note: Also exempts assistive technologies and disability accommodations.

units.passage: Basic deterministic utilities (e.g., calculators, basic rule-based spell/grammar checkers, simple macros, mail-merge).
units.policy: Basic deterministic utilities such as calculators, basic rule-based spell/grammar checkers, simple macros and mail-merge are not AI tools under this policy unless they incorporate AI/ML features.
units.why: The exclusions list says 'basic rule-based spell/grammar checkers' are not AI tools. P100 is the nearest type (routine features outside the rules), though here the reason is that they are not AI.
units.fit_note: A: Exclusion is because the tools are not AI (deterministic), not an exemption of AI features from a restrictive rule. B: Exclusion is a scope definition for non-AI utilities, not an exemption of AI features from a restrictive rule.

units.passage: Many commonly accepted tools have artificial intelligence embedded within to aid in their operation. Unless specifically prohibited, use of these tools is permissible when an individual creates content and applies the tool to refine their work. Examples include: spelling and grammar programs, search engines, and navigation maps
units.policy: Unless specifically prohibited, use of these AI-embedded tools is permissible when an individual creates content and applies the tool to refine their work.
units.why: The Assistive AI definition says "Unless specifically prohibited, use of these tools is permissible when an individual creates content and applies the tool to refine their work", exempting embedded routine features such as spelling, search and maps, which is P100.

units.passage: b.) appropriately acknowledge the use of GAI that contributed to their work even if that information is not in their final submission. In instances where the use of GAI is restricted or prohibited, it is recognized that certain standard tools may be embedded with Assistive AI technology and these may be used unless specifically prohibited. In instances where use of GAI is restricted the instructor will identify in writing those instances, if any, where the technology may be used.
units.why: In restricted or prohibited courses "these may be used unless specifically prohibited": embedded assistive tools stay usable, which is P100.

units.passage: Routine spell-check doesn't require documentation, but if you're unsure whether your use crosses that line, include a brief acknowledgment—it's better to over-document than under-document.
units.why: Exempts routine spell-check from documentation and says to over-disclose when unsure: P100.
units.fit_note: Also says over-document when unsure. Also says to include an acknowledgment when unsure.
